table.text: All methods were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board (IRB #15744: "Examining Differences in Cognitive Reappraisal Efficacy for Spanish-English Bilinguals").

In 2024, we recruited 250 U.S.-based Spanish-English bilingual women who reported learning Spanish before (78.4%) or concurrently with English (21.6%) and demonstrated high Spanish and English proficiency.

Participants were presented with negative images before hearing audio recordings either describing the negative contents of the image or reinterpreting those contents to be less negative (i.e., social reappraisal) in either Spanish or English.

Third, Quiñones-Camacho et al. (2019) found that Spanish-English bilinguals reported using cognitive reappraisal more in English (L2) than in Spanish (L1) and that the impact of emotion regulation on physiology depended on the language participants were speaking.

table.text: Pre-registered inclusion criteria included: living in the United States, a 95% or higher approval rating on previous studies (calculated by Prolific), being 18-39 years old, identifying as women, reporting Spanish as an earliest learned language -all of which were prescreened by Prolificand passing an auditory language translation quiz that ensured adequate proficiency to comprehend study materials (see Language Experience and Proficiency Screener below).
Participants were first screened for language experience via Prolific where they responded to the following question: "What language(s) did you speak earliest in life?"

Participants completed a subset of questions from the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q) in English, which is a validated tool for collecting self-reported proficiency and language history (Kaushanskaya et al., 2020; Marian et al., 2007).

Before beginning the task, participants were asked to select where 0 and 100 were represented on the scale.
Participants were warned that they would have limited time to make their rating, and an image of a red square would appear at the bottom of the affect rating scale if they were too slow.
Participants completed 72 trials of this task (i.e., 18 trials per condition).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: This pre-registered study (https://osf.io/yufqs) was conducted via the Prolific platform in 2024. Because there has been no prior work on the present research question, we conducted a power analysis to ensure 80% power to detect a small effect (Cohen's d = 0.2). This test, implemented with the "pwr.t.test" (Champely, 2020) function in R (R Core Team, 2026), indicated that 198 participants were required. We pre-registered an inflated target N of 250 to provide additional power to detect effects that may have been smaller in size. An initial set of participants (N = 674) completed a screener that assessed inclusion criteria for the study.

Note that the sample size of sequential bilinguals(n = 196) used in this test is smaller than the N we pre-registered in our power analysis to have 80% power to detect effects as large as d = .20 (i.e., n = 198). That said, it is only 2 participants short from this target, and power analyses show that this sample grants 79.6% power to detect small effects (d = .20) and 80% power to detect effects as small as d = .201. Notably, the effect size we do observe for this effect (d = .07; a within-person shift of seven one-hundredths of a standard deviation) is far smaller than this effect size of interest, and the average difference in reappraisal success we observe is a numerical shift of 0.7 points on a one-hundred point scale. In fact, if the population effect is truly d = .07, that would require 1,604 participants to detect with 80% power.

This analysis returned main effects of both Audio Content, F(1, 13524) = 1432.96, p < .001, ηp² = .10, 90% CI [.09, .11], and Language, F(1, 13524) = 11.14, p < .001, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, .002], but no interaction between them, F(1, 13524) = 0.66, p = .416, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, < .001]. To provide a common-sense estimate of the impact of Language on reappraisal within this subsample, we computed a Cohen's d effect size for the difference in reappraisal efficacy across Spanish and English conditions. We computed participant-level mean differences in ratings for Spanish Describe and Spanish Reappraise trials, as well as participant-level mean differences in ratings for English Describe and English Reappraise trials, and then we measured the size of the within-subjects difference across these two estimates of "reappraisal success" in each language. This difference was very small (d = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.21]), with reappraisal success numerically larger in English (M = 15.01) than Spanish (M = 14.31). Thus, if there is any effect within this subsample, it is extremely small (seven one-hundredths of a standard-deviation change within-persons) and would require 1,604 participants to detect with 80% power. Although this is a post-hoc test in just a subsample of participants (see footnote 3 in the primary article for a discussion of power), this result again aligns with hypothesis 3c: There is no compelling evidence that reappraisal success differs between L1 and L2 in Spanish-English bilinguals, even when restricting to sequential bilinguals only.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Examining differences in social reappraisal efficacy across first- and second-language in Spanish-English bilinguals
table.research_questions:
Bilingualism — the use of two languages in everyday life — is an increasingly common linguistic experience for children worldwide (Byers-Heinlein et al., 2019). Bilingual children receive input from both their first language chronologically acquired (L1) and their second language (L2) as they begin to learn about emotions and emotion regulation. Some studies on adult bilinguals have found that emotional response to stimuli (self-reported or measured physiologically) is more intense when presented in L1 compared to in L2 (Chen et al., 2012; Dylman & Bjärtå, 2018; Harris, 2004; Harris et al., 2003, 2006). However, we know little about how emotion regulation differs in L1 vs. L2 for bilinguals. Emotion regulation refers to the processes by which individuals influence how they experience and express emotions (Gross, 1998). To date, scholars have shown that self-reported distress decreases when Swedish (L1)-English (L2) bilinguals switched from reading in L1 to answering questions in L2, consistent with prior work showing reduced intensity of emotions in L2 than L1 (Dylman & Bjärtå, 2018). Additionally, Spanish-English bilinguals reported using cognitive reappraisal (i.e., changing one’s interpretation of a stimulus to change one’s emotions), more often in English than in Spanish (Quiñones-Camacho et al., 2019), suggesting that people may choose more “cognitive” emotion regulation strategies in L2 than L1 contexts. 

However, studies have yet to experimentally compare how the efficacy of the same emotion regulation strategy differs in a bilingual person’s first or second language. Testing this research question can further our understanding of how the bilingual experience affects emotional learning and processing, with implications for how we can provide better emotional education and support to bilingual populations. The current study manipulates the language in which Spanish-English bilinguals hear cognitive reappraisals of negative images and examines if one language is more effective than the other (Spanish vs. English) at alleviating (self-reported) negative affect. Recruited participants will be aged 18–39, based in the United States, with a history of learning Spanish first and English second (or concurrently). Due to possible neural differences in the use of cognitive reappraisal between genders (McRae et al., 2008; Sahi et al., 2023), only participants who identify as women will be recruited. Participants will have to pass a Spanish-English translation quiz to ensure sufficient proficiency in both languages before moving on to the formal study. Demographics, language history data, and self-reported language proficiency levels will also be collected.

Our primary hypotheses are as follows:
1) Participants will on average report more negative affect on Describe trials compared to Reappraise trials, regardless of language. This finding would replicate prior work on the effect of cognitive reappraisal in reducing negative emotions.
2) Participants will on average report more negative affect in Spanish trials compared to English trials, regardless of the contents of the audio clips (i.e., Describe or Reappraise). This finding would replicate previous research findings of L1 producing more intense emotional responses than L2.
3) We do not have a clear prediction regarding the interaction of language and audio contents; there are three possible alternative hypotheses:
          3.1) Participants may show greater cognitive reappraisal efficacy in L1 than in L2. If so, this would imply that regulation is more effective in Spanish than in English due to greater fluency and/or familiarity with reappraisal and emotion regulation in the language they learned first. 
          3.2) Participants may show greater cognitive reappraisal efficacy in L2 than in L1. If so, this would imply that regulation is more effective in English than in Spanish due to increased emotional distance (i.e., reduced intensity of emotions) in L2.
          3.3) No interaction may emerge. This would imply that cognitive reappraisal efficacy is equivalent in L1 and L2.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: The study deploys a 2 [Language: Spanish vs. English] x 2 [Audio Content: Describe vs. Reappraise] within-subject paradigm adapted from a previous study on cognitive reappraisal (Sahi et al., 2021). Participants will view 72 negative images evenly distributed across the four resulting conditions. To minimize the need to switch between languages, trials will be grouped into Spanish and English blocks, with the order of these blocks counterbalanced across participants. Within each block, the order of “Describe” and “Reappraise” trials is randomized. “Describe” trials will have participants listening to factual descriptions of the negative images, and “Reappraise” trials will have participants listening to positive cognitive reappraisals of the images. Following each trial, participants will rate their negative affect on a scale of 0–100 (0 = “not bad at all”; 100 = “very bad”). Note that the task instructions are explained in English for all subjects, but the rating scale is presented without any words (just 0–100) so it is equivalent across Spanish and English blocks. We will analyze negative affect ratings in each condition to determine whether cognitive reappraisal is more effective in Spanish or English at reducing participants’ negative affect. To ensure condition differences are attributable to our task’s factors (and not specific images or audio recordings), we have created 4 matched lists of images each with 4 matched sets of audio recordings (i.e., English Describe, English Reappraise, Spanish Describe, and Spanish Reappraise), and we will counterbalance participants to image/audio set.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: The target demographic will be 18–39 year-old, Spanish (L1) and English (L2 or concurrent L1) bilingual speakers who identify as a woman, based in the United States. People outside of this demographic will be excluded. Participants will be recruited from the online platform Prolific, must have a 95% or higher approval rating on previous studies (calculated by Prolific) to be included. Screener participants will be excluded if they fail to pass the language translation quiz that ensures a minimum proficiency level in Spanish and English to comprehend study materials. Participants who do pass the screener will be invited within a week to take part in the study trials; all communication will be through the platform Prolific.
table.sample_size: We aim to have a final sample of 250 usable participants for our primary analysis.
table.sample_size_rationale: Because prior work has never tested this specific comparison, we conducted our power analyses using a small Cohen’s d of 0.2. Using the “pwr.t.test” in R (R Core Team, 2022), we found that 198 participants were required for 80% power to detect a main effect of d = 0.2. We inflated this target N to 250 to provide additional power to assess interaction and other effects including the exploratory moderations described below.
table.stopping_rule: Given that exclusion criteria may lead us to exclude participants after they have participated, we will recruit participants in waves. We will aim to have 250 usable participants but the size of the final wave and proportion we have to exclude may lead to a small number more than this target. But we will stop when the last wave provides at least 250 usable participants.
table.manipulated_variables: There are four conditions in total: a “Describe” condition and a “Reappraise” condition in two languages, Spanish and English. Participants in this within-subjects design will have trials of “Describe” and “Reappraise” conditions in both Spanish and English. The “Describe” trials have participants listening to audio clips factually describing the contents of the image stimuli, with the audio in either Spanish or English. The “Reappraise” trials will involve audio clips of cognitive reappraisals of the image stimuli. The order of the Spanish and English blocks will be counterbalanced across participants, while the order of “Describe” and “Reappraise” trials in each block will be randomized for each participant. The stimuli used in the four groups will be distributed such that average valence and arousal ratings of the images do not differ significantly between conditions, and assignment of stimulus list to condition is counterbalanced across participants.
table.measured_variables:
There is one primary dependent variable from the emotion regulation task: negative affect ratings. Participants will rate their negative affect on a slider, in response to seeing negative images and hearing audio clips that either describe the image factually or reappraise the image. The slider will have a scale of 0–100 (0 = “not bad at all”, 100 = “very bad”). There will be a total of 72 ratings for each participant, and 18 per condition (2 [Language: Spanish vs. English] x 2 [Audio Content: Describe vs. Reappraise]). We will average these ratings per condition. 

Other key variables assess Spanish and English language proficiency and dominance. We will also collect participants’ self-reported proficiency, where they will rate their level of proficiency in speaking, understanding (listening), and reading Spanish and English each on a scale of 0–10 (0 = “none”, 10 = “perfect”). The three scores for each language will be averaged for an overall proficiency score. Considering this study’s usage of audio clips, the understanding (listening) scores in Spanish and English specifically may also be separately used in exploratory analyses.

We will collect additional data from participants: (1) age of acquisition of L1 and L2, (2) languages ranked in order of dominance, and (3) questionnaire data (e.g., Bilingual Switching Questionnaire, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, Patient Health Questionnaire 8, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder 8). In particular, the Bilingual Switching Questionnaire measures participants' tendencies to switch from one language to another (switch to L1 and switch to L2). Earlier acquisition and/or greater proficiency in one language is correlated with fewer switches to the other language (Rodriguez-Fornells et al., 2012). We collect these data for exploratory follow-up analyses. We will transparently report in the final paper that analyses of these DVs are exploratory in nature.
table.statistical_tests: Analyses will be conducted using R. We will test our primary hypotheses by performing a 2 × 2 ANOVA to quantify how Language (L1 vs. L2) and Audio Content (Describe vs. Reappraise) factors affect negative affect ratings. We will follow-up a significant interaction of language and audio content with condition-wise t-tests.
table.inference_criteria: Our alpha level is set to .05, and tests will be two-tailed.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Data from participants who fail the CAPTCHA bot check or both attention checks (there are two, one in the Spanish block and one in the English block) will be excluded. If participants only fail one attention check, we will do a qualitative check on their responses to open-ended questions (i.e., mandatory feedback form) to evaluate their attentiveness before deciding to exclude them. In addition, given that the trials auto-advance, we will exclude any participant who fails to respond to more than 50% of trials in any condition. Finally, participants who leave midway through the study due to language comprehension issues or psychological discomfort will be compensated for their time but will be excluded from data analysis.
table.missing_data_handling:
Within the task, we will compute average ratings within each condition. Missing trials will be ignored in these averages (though we exclude anyone who does not respond to more than 50% of trials in a condition).

If participants do not provide data for supplementary analyses (e.g., proficiency questions), we will exclude them only from analyses of those specific data.
table.exploratory_analyses: We will explore using measures of proficiency, age of L2 acquisition, self-reported language dominance, and language-switching frequency scores as possible moderators in the ANOVA. For example, we can test whether the benefits of L1 vs L2 reappraisal vary depending on whether participants report English or Spanish as their currently ‘dominant’ language by adding it as a factor in the ANOVA and testing for a 3-way interaction in the ANOVA: 2 [Language] x 2 [Content] x 2 [Dominance]. Similarly, participants can be divided into two groups based on age of L2 acquisition (before the age of 12 [i.e. early to middle childhood] and after 12); three groups based on proficiency (L1 > L2, L1 = L2, and L1 < L2); and three groups based on language-switching frequency (more switches to L1, equal frequency of switching, and more switches to L2). If there are significant interactions, we will follow up with more fine-grained analyses to unpack what is driving the effect.

We recommend manually checking the full preregistration at the link above, and have provided the preregistered sample size. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(id = "yufqs", sample_size = "We aim to have a final sample of 250 usable participants for our primary analysis."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Full Preregistration" collapse="true"} ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Field = c("template_name", "title", "id", "link", "date_created", "date_modified", "date_registered", "embargo_end_date", "ia_url", "research_questions", "study_type", "blinding", "study_design_overview", "existing_data", "data_collection_procedures", "sample_size", "sample_size_rationale", "stopping_rule", "manipulated_variables", "measured_variables", "statistical_tests", "inference_criteria", "data_exclusion_criteria", "missing_data_handling", "exploratory_analyses", "additional_comments", "paper_id"), "Preregistration 1" = c("OSF Preregistration", "Examining differences in social reappraisal efficacy across first- and second-language in Spanish-English bilinguals", "yufqs", "https://osf.io/yufqs", "2024-02-20T22:52:39.885829", "2024-02-20T22:51:17.128226", "2024-02-20T22:52:39.858311", "", "https://archive.org/details/osf-registrations-yufqs-v1", "Bilingualism — the use of two languages in everyday life — is an increasingly common linguistic experience for children worldwide (Byers-Heinlein et al., 2019). Bilingual children receive input from both their first language chronologically acquired (L1) and their second language (L2) as they begin to learn about emotions and emotion regulation. Some studies on adult bilinguals have found that emotional response to stimuli (self-reported or measured physiologically) is more intense when presented in L1 compared to in L2 (Chen et al., 2012; Dylman & Bjärtå, 2018; Harris, 2004; Harris et al., 2003, 2006). However, we know little about how emotion regulation differs in L1 vs. L2 for bilinguals. Emotion regulation refers to the processes by which individuals influence how they experience and express emotions (Gross, 1998). To date, scholars have shown that self-reported distress decreases when Swedish (L1)-English (L2) bilinguals switched from reading in L1 to answering questions in L2, consistent with prior work showing reduced intensity of emotions in L2 than L1 (Dylman & Bjärtå, 2018). Additionally, Spanish-English bilinguals reported using cognitive reappraisal (i.e., changing one’s interpretation of a stimulus to change one’s emotions), more often in English than in Spanish (Quiñones-Camacho et al., 2019), suggesting that people may choose more “cognitive” emotion regulation strategies in L2 than L1 contexts.

However, studies have yet to experimentally compare how the efficacy of the same emotion regulation strategy differs in a bilingual person’s first or second language. Testing this research question can further our understanding of how the bilingual experience affects emotional learning and processing, with implications for how we can provide better emotional education and support to bilingual populations. The current study manipulates the language in which Spanish-English bilinguals hear cognitive reappraisals of negative images and examines if one language is more effective than the other (Spanish vs. English) at alleviating (self-reported) negative affect. Recruited participants will be aged 18–39, based in the United States, with a history of learning Spanish first and English second (or concurrently). Due to possible neural differences in the use of cognitive reappraisal between genders (McRae et al., 2008; Sahi et al., 2023), only participants who identify as women will be recruited. Participants will have to pass a Spanish-English translation quiz to ensure sufficient proficiency in both languages before moving on to the formal study. Demographics, language history data, and self-reported language proficiency levels will also be collected.

Our primary hypotheses are as follows:
1) Participants will on average report more negative affect on Describe trials compared to Reappraise trials, regardless of language. This finding would replicate prior work on the effect of cognitive reappraisal in reducing negative emotions.
2) Participants will on average report more negative affect in Spanish trials compared to English trials, regardless of the contents of the audio clips (i.e., Describe or Reappraise). This finding would replicate previous research findings of L1 producing more intense emotional responses than L2.
3) We do not have a clear prediction regarding the interaction of language and audio contents; there are three possible alternative hypotheses:
3.1) Participants may show greater cognitive reappraisal efficacy in L1 than in L2. If so, this would imply that regulation is more effective in Spanish than in English due to greater fluency and/or familiarity with reappraisal and emotion regulation in the language they learned first.
3.2) Participants may show greater cognitive reappraisal efficacy in L2 than in L1. If so, this would imply that regulation is more effective in English than in Spanish due to increased emotional distance (i.e., reduced intensity of emotions) in L2.
3.3) No interaction may emerge. This would imply that cognitive reappraisal efficacy is equivalent in L1 and L2.", "Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.", "No blinding is involved in this study.", "The study deploys a 2 [Language: Spanish vs. English] x 2 [Audio Content: Describe vs. Reappraise] within-subject paradigm adapted from a previous study on cognitive reappraisal (Sahi et al., 2021). Participants will view 72 negative images evenly distributed across the four resulting conditions. To minimize the need to switch between languages, trials will be grouped into Spanish and English blocks, with the order of these blocks counterbalanced across participants. Within each block, the order of “Describe” and “Reappraise” trials is randomized. “Describe” trials will have participants listening to factual descriptions of the negative images, and “Reappraise” trials will have participants listening to positive cognitive reappraisals of the images. Following each trial, participants will rate their negative affect on a scale of 0–100 (0 = “not bad at all”; 100 = “very bad”). Note that the task instructions are explained in English for all subjects, but the rating scale is presented without any words (just 0–100) so it is equivalent across Spanish and English blocks. We will analyze negative affect ratings in each condition to determine whether cognitive reappraisal is more effective in Spanish or English at reducing participants’ negative affect. To ensure condition differences are attributable to our task’s factors (and not specific images or audio recordings), we have created 4 matched lists of images each with 4 matched sets of audio recordings (i.e., English Describe, English Reappraise, Spanish Describe, and Spanish Reappraise), and we will counterbalance participants to image/audio set.", "Registration prior to creation of data", "The target demographic will be 18–39 year-old, Spanish (L1) and English (L2 or concurrent L1) bilingual speakers who identify as a woman, based in the United States. People outside of this demographic will be excluded. Participants will be recruited from the online platform Prolific, must have a 95% or higher approval rating on previous studies (calculated by Prolific) to be included. Screener participants will be excluded if they fail to pass the language translation quiz that ensures a minimum proficiency level in Spanish and English to comprehend study materials. Participants who do pass the screener will be invited within a week to take part in the study trials; all communication will be through the platform Prolific.", "We aim to have a final sample of 250 usable participants for our primary analysis.", "Because prior work has never tested this specific comparison, we conducted our power analyses using a small Cohen’s d of 0.2. Using the “pwr.t.test” in R (R Core Team, 2022), we found that 198 participants were required for 80% power to detect a main effect of d = 0.2. We inflated this target N to 250 to provide additional power to assess interaction and other effects including the exploratory moderations described below.", "Given that exclusion criteria may lead us to exclude participants after they have participated, we will recruit participants in waves. We will aim to have 250 usable participants but the size of the final wave and proportion we have to exclude may lead to a small number more than this target. But we will stop when the last wave provides at least 250 usable participants.", "There are four conditions in total: a “Describe” condition and a “Reappraise” condition in two languages, Spanish and English. Participants in this within-subjects design will have trials of “Describe” and “Reappraise” conditions in both Spanish and English. The “Describe” trials have participants listening to audio clips factually describing the contents of the image stimuli, with the audio in either Spanish or English. The “Reappraise” trials will involve audio clips of cognitive reappraisals of the image stimuli. The order of the Spanish and English blocks will be counterbalanced across participants, while the order of “Describe” and “Reappraise” trials in each block will be randomized for each participant. The stimuli used in the four groups will be distributed such that average valence and arousal ratings of the images do not differ significantly between conditions, and assignment of stimulus list to condition is counterbalanced across participants.", "There is one primary dependent variable from the emotion regulation task: negative affect ratings. Participants will rate their negative affect on a slider, in response to seeing negative images and hearing audio clips that either describe the image factually or reappraise the image. The slider will have a scale of 0–100 (0 = “not bad at all”, 100 = “very bad”). There will be a total of 72 ratings for each participant, and 18 per condition (2 [Language: Spanish vs. English] x 2 [Audio Content: Describe vs. Reappraise]). We will average these ratings per condition.

Other key variables assess Spanish and English language proficiency and dominance. We will also collect participants’ self-reported proficiency, where they will rate their level of proficiency in speaking, understanding (listening), and reading Spanish and English each on a scale of 0–10 (0 = “none”, 10 = “perfect”). The three scores for each language will be averaged for an overall proficiency score. Considering this study’s usage of audio clips, the understanding (listening) scores in Spanish and English specifically may also be separately used in exploratory analyses.

We will collect additional data from participants: (1) age of acquisition of L1 and L2, (2) languages ranked in order of dominance, and (3) questionnaire data (e.g., Bilingual Switching Questionnaire, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, Patient Health Questionnaire 8, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder 8). In particular, the Bilingual Switching Questionnaire measures participants' tendencies to switch from one language to another (switch to L1 and switch to L2). Earlier acquisition and/or greater proficiency in one language is correlated with fewer switches to the other language (Rodriguez-Fornells et al., 2012). We collect these data for exploratory follow-up analyses. We will transparently report in the final paper that analyses of these DVs are exploratory in nature.", "Analyses will be conducted using R. We will test our primary hypotheses by performing a 2 × 2 ANOVA to quantify how Language (L1 vs. L2) and Audio Content (Describe vs. Reappraise) factors affect negative affect ratings. We will follow-up a significant interaction of language and audio content with condition-wise t-tests.", "Our alpha level is set to .05, and tests will be two-tailed.", "Data from participants who fail the CAPTCHA bot check or both attention checks (there are two, one in the Spanish block and one in the English block) will be excluded. If participants only fail one attention check, we will do a qualitative check on their responses to open-ended questions (i.e., mandatory feedback form) to evaluate their attentiveness before deciding to exclude them. In addition, given that the trials auto-advance, we will exclude any participant who fails to respond to more than 50% of trials in any condition. Finally, participants who leave midway through the study due to language comprehension issues or psychological discomfort will be compensated for their time but will be excluded from data analysis.", "Within the task, we will compute average ratings within each condition. Missing trials will be ignored in these averages (though we exclude anyone who does not respond to more than 50% of trials in a condition).

If participants do not provide data for supplementary analyses (e.g., proficiency questions), we will exclude them only from analyses of those specific data.", "We will explore using measures of proficiency, age of L2 acquisition, self-reported language dominance, and language-switching frequency scores as possible moderators in the ANOVA. For example, we can test whether the benefits of L1 vs L2 reappraisal vary depending on whether participants report English or Spanish as their currently ‘dominant’ language by adding it as a factor in the ANOVA and testing for a 3-way interaction in the ANOVA: 2 [Language] x 2 [Content] x 2 [Dominance]. Similarly, participants can be divided into two groups based on age of L2 acquisition (before the age of 12 [i.e. early to middle childhood] and after 12); three groups based on proficiency (L1 > L2, L1 = L2, and L1 < L2); and three groups based on language-switching frequency (more switches to L1, equal frequency of switching, and more switches to L2). If there are significant interactions, we will follow up with more fine-grained analyses to unpack what is driving the effect.", "References

stat_check.title: StatCheck
stat_check.summary_text: We detected no errors in t-tests or F-tests.

table.text: A pilot version of the study was conducted on Prolific with a separate sample of 12 participants to ensure that reappraisals produced lower negative affect than descriptions across both languages before proceeding to collect data for the main study, F(1, 715.20) = 73.16, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.06, .13].
table.formatted: A pilot version of the study was conducted on Prolific with a separate sample of 12 participants to ensure that reappraisals produced lower negative affect than descriptions across both languages before proceeding to collect data for the main study, F(1, 715.20) = 73.16, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.06, .13].

table.text: A mixed-effects analysis of trial-level negative affect ratings indicated a significant main effect of Audio Content, F(1, 17262) = 1788.04, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.09, .10], such that participants reported greater negative affect on Describe trials compared to Reappraise trials (Figure 2).
table.formatted: A mixed-effects analysis of trial-level negative affect ratings indicated a significant main effect of Audio Content, F(1, 17262) = 1788.04, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.09, .10], such that participants reported greater negative affect on Describe trials compared to Reappraise trials (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

table.text: Follow-up analyses within English trials demonstrated higher negative affect for English Describe (M = 41.11, SD = 32.11) than English Reappraise (M = 26.16, SD = 27.21) trials, F(1, 8477.5) = 968.66, p < .001, ηp² = .10, 90% CI [.09, .11].
table.formatted: Follow-up analyses within English trials demonstrated higher negative affect for English Describe (M = 41.11, SD = 32.11) than English Reappraise (M = 26.16, SD = 27.21) trials, F(1, 8477.5) = 968.66, p < .001, ηp² = .10, 90% CI [.09, .11].

table.text: Similarly, within Spanish trials, we found higher negative affect on Spanish Describe (M = 41.70, SD = 31.82) than Spanish Reappraise (M = 27.54, SD = 28.01) trials, F(1, 8468.3) = 850.31, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.08, .10].
table.formatted: Similarly, within Spanish trials, we found higher negative affect on Spanish Describe (M = 41.70, SD = 31.82) than Spanish Reappraise (M = 27.54, SD = 28.01) trials, F(1, 8468.3) = 850.31, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.08, .10].

table.text: We also observed a significant effect of Language, F(1, 17262) = 8.86, p = .003, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, .001].
table.formatted: We also observed a significant effect of Language, F(1, 17262) = 8.86, p = .003, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, .001].

table.text: We found no significant interaction between these factors, (F(1, 17262) = 1.02, p = .313), ηp² < .001, 90% CI [.00, < .001], indicating that the effect of Audio Content (i.e., Describe versus Reappraise) on participants' negative affect was not significantly different between the two languages.

table.text: When analyzing condition means for each participant, an ANOVA returned a significant main effect of Audio Content on participants' negative affect, F(1, 249) = 374.59, p < .001, ηp² = .60, 90% CI [.54, .65], such that participants reported a higher negative affect on Describe trials than on Reappraise trials.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .837", "ps > .130", "p ≤ .05", 
"p < .05"), Text = c("T-tests for all pairwise comparisons produced ps > .837, and all 95% confidence intervals included zero, indicating no reliable differences between sets (see Table S3 for values).", 
"All t-tests produced ps > .130, and all 95% confidence intervals included zero, indicating no reliable differences between sets (see Tables S2 and S4 for details).", 
"All uncorrected p-values that do not survive correction are.01 ≤ p ≤ .05 and their effects are extremely small (i.e., ηp² ≤ .001, save for one moderator main effect that is larger).", 
"Table S6: Statistics for moderator interactions with uncorrected p < .05."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 119 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

13 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

78 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **49 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In 2024, we recruited 250 U.S.-based Spanish-English bilingual women who reported learning Spanish before (78.4%) or concurrently with English (21.6%) and demonstrated high Spanish and English proficiency.

Participants were presented with negative images before hearing audio recordings either describing the negative contents of the image or reinterpreting those contents to be less negative (i.e., social reappraisal) in either Spanish or English.

Third, Quiñones-Camacho et al. (2019) found that Spanish-English bilinguals reported using cognitive reappraisal more in English (L2) than in Spanish (L1) and that the impact of emotion regulation on physiology depended on the language participants were speaking.
This pre-registered study (https://osf.io/yufqs) was conducted via the Prolific platform in 2024.
This test, implemented with the "pwr.t.test" (Champely, 2020) function in R (R Core Team, 2026), indicated that 198 participants were required.

Pre-registered inclusion criteria included: living in the United States, a 95% or higher approval rating on previous studies (calculated by Prolific), being 18-39 years old, identifying as women, reporting Spanish as an earliest learned language -all of which were prescreened by Prolificand passing an auditory language translation quiz that ensured adequate proficiency to comprehend study materials (see Language Experience and Proficiency Screener below).
Participants were first screened for language experience via Prolific where they responded to the following question: "What language(s) did you speak earliest in life?"

Participants completed a subset of questions from the Language Experience and Proficiency Questionnaire (LEAP-Q) in English, which is a validated tool for collecting self-reported proficiency and language history (Kaushanskaya et al., 2020; Marian et al., 2007).

As part of this assessment, participants provided a list of languages they knew in order of dominance and order of acquisition, language proficiency ratings, and age of immigration to the U.S. (if applicable).
Only participants who received a perfect score on this translation quiz (74% of people who completed the quiz) were invited through Prolific to participate in the full study.
Participants completed the emotion regulation task and questionnaires via Gorilla (https://gorilla.sc/), an online experiment builder for implementing behavioral tasks and surveys.

Before beginning the study, participants completed a CAPTCHA attention check (i.e., writing visually degraded numbers into text boxes) and audio check (i.e., hearing the word "decimal" and writing the word into a text box).
Participants completed a social reappraisal task adapted from prior research (Sahi et al., 2021 (Sahi et al.,, 2025)).
After viewing the image and listening to the clip, participants had 4 seconds to rate how bad they felt on a sliding scale ranging from 0 to 100.
Before beginning the task, participants were asked to select where 0 and 100 were represented on the scale.
Participants were warned that they would have limited time to make their rating, and an image of a red square would appear at the bottom of the affect rating scale if they were too slow.
Participants completed 72 trials of this task (i.e., 18 trials per condition).

To minimize any potential language-switching costs in auditory comprehension (Olson, 2017), trials were grouped into Spanish and English blocks such that participants completed all Spanish trials contiguously and all English trials contiguously.

Trials were auto-advancing, and we included two attention checks randomly interspersed through the task in which participants had to drag a specified number from a list of numbers into a dropzone and submit.

A pilot version of the study was conducted on Prolific with a separate sample of 12 participants to ensure that reappraisals produced lower negative affect than descriptions across both languages before proceeding to collect data for the main study, F(1, 715.20) = 73.16, p < .001, ηp² = .09, 90% CI [.06, .13].
After the task, participants completed a set of questionnaires in English assessing demographics and relevant traits that could moderate our effects.
Participants completed this 8-item measure of depressive symptoms over the last two weeks (e.g., "feeling down, depressed, or hopeless;" Kroenke et al., 2009).

The primary pre-registered outcome measures for each participant were their negative affect ratings averaged within the task's four conditions: Spanish Describe, Spanish Reappraise, English Describe, and English Reappraise.

(2012) German-French (n=20) and French-German (n=21) 41 German-French Bilinguals: Intensity = 5.2, French-German Bilinguals: Intensity = 4.3 German-French Bilinguals: Proficiency = 74.5/ 100, AoA = 10.8, Intensity = 3.4, French-German Bilinguals: Proficiency = 72.4/100, AoA = 12.3, Intensity = 4.8 Affective priming effects were consistently found in L1, but only emerged in L2 when participants had high L2 language use and immersion.

Note, to access the study at all, participants must have answered "Spanish" to Prolific's demographics question regarding "What language(s) did you speak earliest in life?", providing initial filtering to ensure Spanish was one of our participants' earliest languages.

For thoroughness, we utilized additional measures that we had collected that were relevant to this research question (L1 age of acquisition, whether participants were simultaneous bilinguals [reported learning English concurrently with Spanish] or sequential bilinguals [reported learning English after Spanish], trait use of cognitive reappraisal in daily life, depression symptoms, and anxiety symptoms).

Age of acquisition and proficiency for each language, as well as dominance and whether participants were simultaneous or sequential bilinguals were all assessed using the adapted LEAP-Q presented in Supplemental Section I (proficiency is the average of the reading, speaking, and understanding items).
Although this exclusion criterion was not pre-registered, adding it provides additional confidence that participants were attentive and honest in their reporting.

We conducted a non-pre-registered analysis testing whether the order in which participants completed English versus Spanish blocks affected their responses.
Thus, the main effects of Content and Language were not attributable to which language participants completed first.

However, the lack of a three-way interaction of Content × Language × Language Block Order indicates that the main effects of Content and Language were not attributable to which language participants completed first.
We added this for additional certainty that participants were attentive and honest.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("DataAnalysis_R2.Rmd", "DataAnalysis_R2.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "DataAnalysis_R2.Rmd"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `DataAnalysis_R2.R` after `DataAnalysis_R2.Rmd`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**2 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("DataAnalysis_R2.Rmd", "DataAnalysis_R2.R"
)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "DataAnalysis_R2.Rmd", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "~/Google Drive/Shared drives/LEmoLab/LEmoLab/Projects_Active/Cao_Bilingual/[Study] Data Files + Code/Data_OSF"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

2 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing.
