As we report in the main text, we pre-registered analyzing condition-level means using a standard 2 × 2 ANOVA.
However, after completing the study, we discovered that mixed-effects analyses of trial-level responses (with random effects for image and participant) provide more sensitive tests than ANOVAs.
To provide the most sensitive test possible of our research questions, we report trial-level analyses in the main text and condition-level analyses here.

When analyzing condition means for each participant, an ANOVA returned a significant main effect of Audio Content on participants' negative affect, F(1, 249) = 374.59, p < .001, ηp² = .60, 90% CI [.54, .65], such that participants reported a higher negative affect on Describe trials than on Reappraise trials.
text.formatted: When analyzing condition means for each participant, an ANOVA returned a significant main effect of Audio Content on participants' negative affect, F(1, 249) = 374.59, p < .001, ηp² = .60, 90% CI [.54, .65], such that participants reported a higher negative affect on Describe trials than on Reappraise trials.

text.text: Follow-up t-tests demonstrated significant differences between English Describe and English Reappraise conditions, t(249) = 17.85, p < .001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.97, 1.29], and between Spanish Describe and Spanish Reappraise conditions, t(249) = 17.69, p < .001, d = 1.12, 95% CI [0.96, 1.28].
text.formatted: Follow-up t-tests demonstrated significant differences between English Describe and English Reappraise conditions, t(249) = 17.85, p < .001, d = 1.13, 95% CI [0.97, 1.29], and between Spanish Describe and Spanish Reappraise conditions, t(249) = 17.69, p < .001, d = 1.12, 95% CI [0.96, 1.28].

text.text: There was no significant effect of Language in the condition-level ANOVA, though the result was on the border of significance, F(1, 249) = 3.72, p = .055, ηp² = .01, 90% CI [.00, .05].
This analysis also did not return a significant interaction between Content and Language, F(1, 249) = 1.85, p = .175, ηp² = .007, 90% CI [.00, .03].

We pre-registered exploratory analyses testing whether a set of relevant constructs could moderate task effects: Spanish and English proficiency, age of L2 acquisition, self-reported language dominance, and code-switching (which has 4 subscales).

For thoroughness, we utilized additional measures that we had collected that were relevant to this research question (L1 age of acquisition, whether participants were simultaneous bilinguals [reported learning English concurrently with Spanish] or sequential bilinguals [reported learning English after Spanish], trait use of cognitive reappraisal in daily life, depression symptoms, and anxiety symptoms).
Each moderator was independently added into a trial-level linear mixed-effects model to test for interactions with Language and Audio Content in explaining negative affect scores.
Because this led to a total of 13 analyses, we decided to apply Benjamini-Hochberg p-value correction (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) before interpreting results.
text.formatted: Because this led to a total of 13 analyses, we decided to apply Benjamini-Hochberg p-value correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref> before interpreting results.

text.text: Specifically, we extracted the p-values for each moderator's: main effect, interaction with Audio Content, interaction with Language, and three-way interaction with Audio Content and Language.

We then corrected these p-values, working within each effect (i.e., all the moderator main effect p-values were corrected for the 13 tests of this main effect, then all the moderator × Audio Content p-values were corrected, etc.).
Although we did not state this in the pre-registration, correction seems wise to protect against false positives emerging due to repeated tests.
However, there is debate regarding when to correct for multiple corrections, with scholars disagreeing on whether correction should always, never, or sometimes be applied (Rubin, 2021).
text.formatted: However, there is debate regarding when to correct for multiple corrections, with scholars disagreeing on whether correction should always, never, or sometimes be applied <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Rubin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The similarity in research questions underlying these questions (i.e., does a moderator exist?) and the number of tests conducted motivated us to apply correction and caution against overinterpreting results that do not survive this correction.

Nonetheless, for maximal transparency, we present both corrected and uncorrected p-values in Table S5, ANOVA statistics in Table S6, and visualizations of all results below, even those that did not pass correction.
text.formatted: Nonetheless, for maximal transparency, we present both corrected and uncorrected p-values in Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>, ANOVA statistics in Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>, and visualizations of all results below, even those that did not pass correction.

text.text: We thus present our observations and allow interested readers to draw their own conclusions about the potential role of these moderators, although we ourselves would discourage strong interpretation of results that do not survive correction.
All uncorrected p-values that do not survive correction are.01 ≤ p ≤ .05 and their effects are extremely small (i.e., ηp² ≤ .001, save for one moderator main effect that is larger).
Focused studies with greater power for testing three-way interactions could provide more clarity on the significance, replicability, and size of these effects.

We first begin with results that passed correction for multiple comparisons.

Four moderators showed significant interactions with Audio Content that survived correction for multiple comparisons (English proficiency, English to Spanish code-switching, contextual code-switching, and trait cognitive reappraisal use), and a fifth moderator only showed a significant uncorrected interaction (English age of acquisition).
These effects are visualized in Figure S1 and statistics are provided in Table S6.
text.formatted: These effects are visualized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> and statistics are provided in Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>.

text.text: An interaction with Audio Content indicates that the difference in negative affect across Describe and Reappraise trials was larger for some participants than others.

In other words, these moderators influenced how strongly participants benefitted from social reappraisal in this task, with participants benefitting more if they were less proficient in English (and perhaps learned English Generalized Anxiety Disorder -7 (see Table S6 for statistics).
text.formatted: In other words, these moderators influenced how strongly participants benefitted from social reappraisal in this task, with participants benefitting more if they were less proficient in English (and perhaps learned English Generalized Anxiety Disorder -7 (see Table <ref type="table">S6</ref> for statistics).

text.text: To help interpret these three-way interactions, we calculated a "reappraisal success" variable for each participant, where we subtracted their average negative affect rating on Reappraise trials from their average negative affect rating on Describe trials, separately for English and Spanish trials.
We could then visualize reappraisal success in each language as a function of these moderators (see Figure S2).
text.formatted: We could then visualize reappraisal success in each language as a function of these moderators (see Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: The code-switching patterns suggest that the tendency to switch from English to Spanish (Figure S2A) or to contextually switch when triggered by specific situations, topics, or environments (Figure S2B) is positively associated with reappraisal success in English but not Spanish.
text.formatted: The code-switching patterns suggest that the tendency to switch from English to Spanish (Figure <ref type="figure">S2A</ref>) or to contextually switch when triggered by specific situations, topics, or environments (Figure <ref type="figure">S2B</ref>) is positively associated with reappraisal success in English but not Spanish.

text.text: It is possible that participants at very low levels of these bilingual switching scales benefit slightly more from social reappraisal in Spanish than in English, and this effect may reverse at very high levels of bilingual switching (i.e., when code-switching is high, social reappraisal may be more effective in English than Spanish).

A simple Language × Audio Content interaction also emerged in these models, suggesting that after accounting for these dimensions of code-switching, participants benefitted more from social reappraisal in English than Spanish.
Finally, a simple main effect of contextual switching emerged, suggesting that higher contextual switching was associated overall with higher negative affect ratings, regardless of trial condition.

Visualizing the uncorrected three-way interaction between anxiety symptoms, Language, and Audio Content suggests that participants with high anxiety benefitted more from social reappraisal in English than in Spanish (Figure S2C).
text.formatted: Visualizing the uncorrected three-way interaction between anxiety symptoms, Language, and Audio Content suggests that participants with high anxiety benefitted more from social reappraisal in English than in Spanish (Figure <ref type="figure">S2C</ref>).

text.text: To transparently describe patterns we see in the data, we present reappraisal success (i.e., the difference between a participant's average negative affect rating for Describe vs.
Reappraise trials) according to three moderators that showed significant (uncorrected) three-way interactions, even though none of them survived correction for multiple comparisons.

These results suggest that social reappraisal may be more effective in English than Spanish when participants report A) high tendencies to code-switch from English to Spanish, B) high tendencies to contextually code switch in response to specific prompts or environments, or C) high anxiety symptoms.

text.text: We thus tested if differences in regulation across Spanish and English may emerge specifically in a subsample of participants who reported learning English after Spanish.

We split participants into "simultaneous bilinguals" (i.e., those who reported learning English at the same age as Spanish; n = 54) and "sequential bilinguals" (i.e., those who reported learning English after Spanish; n = 196).
As reported in Table S5, adding this factor did not produce a significant three-way interaction.

text.text: However, we wanted to ensure that the effect does not emerge when just analyzing the subsample of sequential bilinguals.
We thus conducted a non-pre-registered analysis of our primary research question within the n = 196 sequential bilinguals.

This analysis returned main effects of both Audio Content, F(1, 13524) = 1432.96, p < .001, ηp² = .10, 90% CI [.09, .11], and Language, F(1, 13524) = 11.14, p < .001, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, .002], but no interaction between them, F(1, 13524) = 0.66, p = .416, ηp² < .001, 90% CI [< .001, < .001].

text.text: To provide a common-sense estimate of the impact of Language on reappraisal within this subsample, we computed a Cohen's d effect size for the difference in reappraisal efficacy across Spanish and English conditions.

We computed participant-level mean differences in ratings for Spanish Describe and Spanish Reappraise trials, as well as participant-level mean differences in ratings for English Describe and English Reappraise trials, and then we measured the size of the within-subjects difference across these two estimates of "reappraisal success" in each language.
This difference was very small (d = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.21]), with reappraisal success numerically larger in English (M = 15.01) than Spanish (M = 14.31).

Thus, if there is any effect within this subsample, it is extremely small (seven one-hundredths of a standard-deviation change within-persons) and would require 1,604 participants to detect with 80% power.

Although this is a post-hoc test in just a subsample of participants (see footnote 3 in the primary article for a discussion of power), this result again aligns with hypothesis 3c: There is no compelling evidence that reappraisal success differs between L1 and L2 in Spanish-English bilinguals, even when restricting to sequential bilinguals only.
We conducted a non-pre-registered analysis testing whether the order in which participants completed English versus Spanish blocks affected their responses.
Recall that n = 123 participants (49.2%) had English followed by Spanish trials, and n = 127 participants (50.8%) had Spanish followed by English trials.
Language block order was added into a linear mixed-effects model.

Figure1: Task design.
For each trial of the emotion regulation task, participants saw a negative image and heard an audio recording for 6 seconds.
They then gave a negative affect rating within 4 seconds.
The content of the audio clip determined whether it was an English Describe, English Reappraise, Spanish Describe, or Spanish Reappraise trial.
To minimize the burden of switching languages, trials were ordered in language blocks (i.e., they completed all English trials contiguously and all Spanish trials contiguously).
Describe and Reappraise trials were intermixed randomly within each block, and the order of Spanish vs.
English blocks was counterbalanced across participants.
